subject: Biology
description: Neuron — structure (cell body, dendrites, axon), action potential, synapses, neurotransmitters, types of neurons.

questions.stem: The basic functional unit of the NERVOUS SYSTEM is the:
questions.explanation: NEURON = the FUNCTIONAL and STRUCTURAL unit of the nervous system. Specialized cells that TRANSMIT electrical+chemical signals. STRUCTURE: (1) CELL BODY (SOMA) — contains nucleus, cytoplasm, organelles. (2) DENDRITES — branched extensions; RECEIVE signals from other neurons (input). (3) AXON — single long fibre; SENDS signals AWAY from cell body (output). (4) AXON TERMINALS — end of axon; release neurotransmitters at synapses. (5) MYELIN SHEATH — fatty insulating layer around axons (made by Schwann cells in PNS, oligodendrocytes in CNS); speeds signal transmission via SALTATORY CONDUCTION. (6) NODES OF RANVIER — gaps in myelin where signal jumps. SIZE: human brain has ~86 BILLION neurons + similar number of GLIAL cells (support cells). NEURON LENGTHS: from a few µm (interneurons in cortex) to 1+ METRE (sciatic nerve neurons spanning spine to toe). LIFESPAN: most neurons last a LIFETIME — they don't divide (with limited exceptions in hippocampus, olfactory bulb). NEUROGENESIS — adult brain creates ~700 new neurons/day in hippocampus. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'functional unit of nervous system' is a NEET, NCERT-driven SSC 1-mark guarantee.

questions.stem: Which structure CONDUCTS impulses AWAY from the neuron's cell body?
questions.explanation: AXON — single LONG CYLINDRICAL fibre that carries action potentials AWAY from cell body to other neurons / muscles / glands. KEY DISTINCTION: DENDRITES (multiple, short, branched) receive INPUT; AXON (typically one, long) sends OUTPUT. AXON HILLOCK — junction of axon and cell body; site where action potential is INITIATED. AXON TERMINALS (synaptic boutons) — branched ending of axon; release NEUROTRANSMITTERS at SYNAPSES (junctions with target cells). SPEED: signals along axon = ~1 m/s (unmyelinated) to 120 m/s (heavily myelinated, like motor neurons of giant squid or human reflex arc). MYELIN SHEATH — increases conduction speed via SALTATORY CONDUCTION (signal 'jumps' from node to node). DAMAGE TO MYELIN: causes MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS (autoimmune attack on CNS myelin) — one of the most common neurological conditions globally. AXON LENGTHS in humans: longest = sciatic nerve (~1 m, from spinal cord to toe); shortest = ~10 µm in cortex. PYQ FREQUENCY: axon function in NEET, NCERT Class 11, IBPS GA biology — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: The junction between two neurons where signals are transmitted is called:
questions.explanation: SYNAPSE — the JUNCTION where two neurons (or a neuron + muscle/gland) communicate. Term coined by Sir Charles Sherrington (1897, Nobel 1932). TWO TYPES: (1) CHEMICAL SYNAPSE (~99% of synapses) — pre-synaptic neuron releases NEUROTRANSMITTERS (chemicals) into a tiny gap (synaptic cleft, ~20-40 nm); they bind to receptors on post-synaptic neuron, triggering response. (2) ELECTRICAL SYNAPSE — direct ion flow through GAP JUNCTIONS (faster, but less common). KEY NEUROTRANSMITTERS: (a) ACETYLCHOLINE — neuromuscular junction, attention, memory. (b) DOPAMINE — reward, motor control (deficit in Parkinson's). (c) SEROTONIN — mood, sleep (target of SSRIs). (d) GABA — main INHIBITORY neurotransmitter (anxiety drugs target it). (e) GLUTAMATE — main EXCITATORY neurotransmitter. (f) NOREPINEPHRINE — alertness, fight-or-flight. (g) ENDORPHINS — natural pain-relievers. SCALE: human brain has ~10¹⁵ synapses (1,000 trillion). NUMBER GROWS during early childhood, then 'PRUNING' streamlines connections in adolescence. NEUROPLASTICITY: synapses can strengthen/weaken with use → basis of LEARNING and MEMORY. PYQ FREQUENCY: synapse-neurotransmitter Qs in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per paper.

questions.stem: Which neurotransmitter's deficiency causes PARKINSON'S DISEASE?
questions.explanation: PARKINSON'S DISEASE — degenerative disorder caused by LOSS of DOPAMINE-PRODUCING neurons in the SUBSTANTIA NIGRA (a midbrain region). SYMPTOMS: (1) RESTING TREMOR (shaking hands at rest). (2) RIGIDITY (stiff muscles). (3) BRADYKINESIA (slow movement). (4) Postural instability. (5) Late-stage: dementia, depression. ETIOLOGY: ~90% sporadic (cause unknown); 10% genetic. AGE: typically affects people 60+. INDIA: ~7 million affected globally; ~1 million in India. TREATMENT: (1) LEVODOPA (L-DOPA) — converted to dopamine in brain; gold-standard drug. (2) Dopamine agonists. (3) MAO-B inhibitors. (4) DEEP BRAIN STIMULATION (DBS) — surgical, electrodes in brain. (5) PHYSICAL THERAPY. FAMOUS PATIENTS: Muhammad Ali (boxing-induced damage may have contributed), Michael J. Fox, Pope John Paul II, Robin Williams. RELATED DISORDERS: ALZHEIMER'S — primarily ACETYLCHOLINE deficiency + amyloid plaques + tau tangles. HUNTINGTON'S — GABA + acetylcholine deficits. DEPRESSION — SEROTONIN, dopamine, norepinephrine. WORLD PARKINSON'S DAY: 11 April (James Parkinson's birthday, 1755). PYQ FREQUENCY: neurotransmitter-disease links in NEET, AIIMS, SSC GA — 1× per cycle.

questions.explanation: THREE MAIN TYPES OF NEURONS based on FUNCTION: (1) MOTOR (efferent) — carry signals AWAY from CNS to muscles/glands. Cause muscle contraction or hormone release. (2) SENSORY (afferent) — carry signals TOWARD CNS from sensory receptors (eyes, ears, skin, etc.). (3) INTERNEURONS — connect neurons WITHIN the CNS; account for ~99% of human neurons; mostly in brain and spinal cord. MEMORIZATION TIP: 'Motor = Move out (from CNS); Sensory = Sense in (to CNS)'. SOMATIC vs AUTONOMIC: somatic motor = voluntary (skeletal muscles); autonomic motor = involuntary (heart, digestion, glands). MOTOR NEURON DISEASES: (1) ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, Lou Gehrig's disease) — progressive degeneration of motor neurons; Stephen Hawking lived with ALS for 55+ years. (2) SPINAL MUSCULAR ATROPHY (SMA) — pediatric. (3) POLIO — viral attack on motor neurons. REFLEX ARC: simplest neural circuit — sensory neuron → spinal cord → motor neuron → muscle. Bypasses brain for SPEED. EXAMPLE: knee-jerk reflex (patellar tendon → quadriceps contraction). PYQ FREQUENCY: motor/sensory neuron distinction in NEET, NCERT 1-2× per paper.

questions.stem: ACTION POTENTIAL in a neuron is generated by the rapid INFLUX of:
questions.explanation: ACTION POTENTIAL — the brief electrical signal that travels along the axon. PHASES: (1) RESTING POTENTIAL (~−70 mV inside): high K⁺ inside, high Na⁺ outside; maintained by Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump. (2) DEPOLARIZATION: stimulus opens VOLTAGE-GATED Na⁺ CHANNELS → Na⁺ FLOODS IN → membrane potential rises rapidly to ~+30 mV. (3) REPOLARIZATION: Na⁺ channels close; K⁺ channels open → K⁺ FLOWS OUT → potential drops back. (4) HYPERPOLARIZATION: brief overshoot below resting (~−80 mV). (5) RETURN to RESTING via pump. SPEED: fastest in MYELINATED axons (saltatory conduction): 100+ m/s. Unmyelinated: ~1 m/s. ALL-OR-NOTHING PRINCIPLE: action potential either fires fully or not at all (no gradation). REFRACTORY PERIOD: brief moment after firing when neuron can't fire again — ensures one-way propagation. ION-CHANNEL DRUGS: (1) LOCAL ANESTHETICS (lidocaine) — block Na⁺ channels to prevent pain signals. (2) PUFFERFISH TOXIN (tetrodotoxin) — blocks Na⁺ channels (neurotoxic; lethal). NOBEL: HODGKIN & HUXLEY (1963) for working out action potential mechanism using giant squid axon. PYQ FREQUENCY: NEET, AIIMS, NCERT Class 11 — 1× per paper.

questions.stem: Which CRANIAL NERVE is responsible for VISION?
questions.explanation: OPTIC NERVE (Cranial Nerve II) — carries visual information from RETINA to BRAIN. Each eye's optic nerve has ~1.2 million axons. The two optic nerves CROSS partially at the OPTIC CHIASM (nasal halves cross over) — allowing depth perception. 12 PAIRS OF CRANIAL NERVES (memorize for NEET): (I) OLFACTORY — smell. (II) OPTIC — vision. (III) OCULOMOTOR — eye movements (most). (IV) TROCHLEAR — eye movement (one muscle). (V) TRIGEMINAL — facial sensation, chewing. (VI) ABDUCENS — eye lateral movement. (VII) FACIAL — facial expression, taste (anterior tongue). (VIII) VESTIBULOCOCHLEAR — hearing + balance. (IX) GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL — taste (posterior tongue), swallowing. (X) VAGUS — parasympathetic to heart, lungs, digestion. (XI) ACCESSORY — neck muscles. (XII) HYPOGLOSSAL — tongue movement. MNEMONIC: 'On Old Olympus' Towering Top, A Famous Vocal German Viewed A Hop' — first letter of each cranial nerve. KEY NERVES TESTED CLINICALLY: II (visual fields), VII (facial nerve palsy), X (gag reflex), XII (tongue deviation). PYQ FREQUENCY: cranial nerve number-function pairing in NEET 1-2× per paper, AIIMS PG entrance frequent.
